Design and Fabrication of a Dual-Band Microstrip Patch Antenna for 2.4/5 GHz

CST Microwave Studio — Complete Step-by-Step Project Guide

Kipson, we'll develop this as an ECE mini project, starting with the CST simulation and then moving to fabrication and measurement. I'll explain the steps in a beginner-friendly way, including antenna calculations, CST modeling, simulation setup, optimization, and report preparation.

1. Project overview

Project title

Design and Fabrication of a Dual-Band Microstrip Patch Antenna for 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wireless Applications Using CST Microwave Studio

Project objectives

  1. Design a microstrip patch antenna using CST.

  2. Achieve two resonant frequencies near 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.

  3. Analyze return loss, VSWR, impedance, gain, and radiation patterns.

  4. Optimize the antenna dimensions to improve matching.

  5. Fabricate the antenna on a PCB.

  6. Measure the fabricated antenna using a Vector Network Analyzer (VNA).

  7. Compare simulated and measured results.

Basic antenna structure

ee.iitb.ac.in

A conventional microstrip patch antenna consists of:

Part

Function

Radiating patch

Radiates electromagnetic energy

Dielectric substrate

Supports the patch

Ground plane

Provides the return conductor

Microstrip feed

Delivers RF power to the patch

For our dual-band design, we'll use a slotted rectangular patch as the initial structure. A slot perturbs the current path and can introduce an additional resonance. The exact dual-band behavior must be verified and tuned in CST; the starting dimensions below are not guaranteed final results.

4. Antenna design calculations

Before opening CST, calculate the initial dimensions of the rectangular patch.

We will first calculate the patch for the lower resonant frequency, 2.4 GHz. The slot will be introduced afterward to produce the second resonance.

4.1 Design parameters

  • Dielectric constant: ϵr=4.3\epsilon_r = 4.3ϵr​=4.3

  • Substrate thickness: h=1.6 mmh = 1.6\text{ mm}h=1.6 mm

  • Speed of light: c=3×108 m/sc = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}c=3×108 m/s

The approximate patch width is:

W=c2fr2ϵr+1W=\frac{c}{2f_r}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\epsilon_r+1}}W=2fr​c​ϵr​+12​​

Substitute the values:

W=3×1082(2.4×109)24.3+1W=\frac{3\times10^8}{2(2.4\times10^9)} \sqrt{\frac{2}{4.3+1}}W=2(2.4×109)3×108​4.3+12​​
W≈37.9 mm\boxed{W\approx37.9\text{ mm}}W≈37.9 mm​

Initial patch width: 37.9 mm

The effective dielectric constant accounts for the fringing fields around the patch.

ϵeff=ϵr+12+ϵr−12(1+12hW)−1/2\epsilon_{eff}= \frac{\epsilon_r+1}{2} +\frac{\epsilon_r-1}{2} \left(1+\frac{12h}{W}\right)^{-1/2}ϵeff​=2ϵr​+1​+2ϵr​−1​(1+W12h​)−1/2

Using W=37.9 mmW=37.9\text{ mm}W=37.9 mm and h=1.6 mmh=1.6\text{ mm}h=1.6 mm:

ϵeff≈4.02\boxed{\epsilon_{eff}\approx4.02}ϵeff​≈4.02​

Leff≈31.2 mmL_{eff}\approx31.2\text{ mm}Leff​≈31.2 mm

The patch has fringing fields at its radiating edges.

ΔLh=0.412(ϵeff+0.3)(W/h+0.264)(ϵeff−0.258)(W/h+0.8)\frac{\Delta L}{h} =0.412 \frac{(\epsilon_{eff}+0.3)(W/h+0.264)} {(\epsilon_{eff}-0.258)(W/h+0.8)}hΔL​=0.412(ϵeff​−0.258)(W/h+0.8)(ϵeff​+0.3)(W/h+0.264)​

5.2 Conceptual layer arrangement

surboolacsu1978.mystrikingly.com

The structure has three main layers:

  1. Ground plane

    A conducting copper layer on the bottom of the substrate.

  2. FR-4 substrate

    Dielectric layer between the patch and ground.

  3. Slotted radiating patch and microstrip feed

    Copper pattern on the top surface.

13. Create the slot for dual-band operation

Step 8 — Introduce the slot

The slot changes the current distribution on the patch and can create or shift a second resonant mode.

There are different dual-band configurations:

For a beginner-friendly design, a U-slot is a useful candidate. However, the exact U-slot dimensions depend on the substrate, patch geometry, feed, and desired matching.

Suggested approach

  1. Start with the rectangular patch.

  2. Verify its first resonance.

  3. Add a slot.

  4. Check whether a second resonance appears near 5 GHz.

  5. Adjust the slot length, width, and position.

  6. Optimize both bands.

U-slot construction concept

A U-slot has two parallel slot arms and a connecting slot section. The slot is cut into the copper patch, leaving the patch connected around the slot.

A simple parametric U-slot may use:

Parameter

Starting range

Slot width

0.6–1.2 mm

Slot arm length

10–20 mm

Slot separation

8–16 mm

Slot position

Around patch center

Slot depth

Optimize in CST

These are search ranges, not final dimensions. Avoid expecting a specific slot length to guarantee 5 GHz without simulation.

CST construction options

Option A: Boolean subtraction

  1. Create a solid U-shaped slot cutter using three thin rectangular solids.

  2. Position the cutter inside the patch.

  3. Use Boolean → Subtract to remove the slot material from the copper patch.

Option B: 2D planar geometry

  1. Draw the patch as a planar shape.

  2. Draw the slot as a closed profile.

  3. Subtract the slot profile.

  4. Extrude the resulting patch to the copper thickness.

The exact menu names can vary by CST version.

15. Select the solver

Step 10 — Choose a solver

For antenna simulations, CST provides different solver options.

Time Domain Solver

A useful choice for broadband antenna simulations because a single excitation can provide a wide frequency response.

Other options:

  • Frequency Domain Solver — useful for frequency-specific or broadband studies.

  • Integral Equation Solver — applicable to suitable open-region electromagnetic problems.

For this project, choose a solver supported by your CST license and version. Time Domain is a reasonable starting choice for the broadband antenna response.

16. Set boundary conditions

Step 11 — Configure open boundaries

A patch antenna radiates into free space. The simulation needs an open region around the antenna.

my.ece.utah.edu

Procedure

  1. Open boundary settings.

  2. Set X-min and X-max to open or open add space.

  3. Set Y-min and Y-max to open or open add space.

  4. Set Z-min and Z-max to open or open add space.

Use CST's open boundary options and sufficient air spacing. The required distance depends on the frequency, antenna dimensions, and boundary formulation.

For a starting point, use a free-space region with clearance of approximately a quarter wavelength at the lowest frequency from the radiating surfaces, then verify convergence. This is a practical initial setting, not a universal rule.

At 2.4 GHz:

λ0=3×1082.4×109=125 mm\lambda_0=\frac{3\times10^8}{2.4\times10^9} =125\text{ mm}λ0​=2.4×1093×108​=125 mm

A quarter wavelength is approximately:

λ0/4=31.25 mm\lambda_0/4=31.25\text{ mm}λ0​/4=31.25 mm

Check whether CST's boundary padding and open boundary settings provide adequate clearance in all directions.

17. Create the excitation port

Step 12 — Waveguide port

For a microstrip-fed antenna, a waveguide port can be used at the end of the feed line when the port is placed across the feed and the surrounding ground/substrate geometry is correctly represented.

dailymotion.com

Port placement

The port should be located at the end of the microstrip feed, at the substrate edge.

For the proposed feed:

  • Port width: cover the feed and sufficient surrounding transverse region.

  • Port height: extend across the substrate thickness and the necessary region above/below.

  • Port orientation: perpendicular to the direction of propagation along the feed.

Procedure

  1. Select the waveguide port tool.

  2. Select the feed end face.

  3. Define the port dimensions.

  4. Verify the port covers the feed and has a valid return path through the ground plane.

  5. Set the mode to the fundamental mode where applicable.

  6. Create the port.

Important: A port placed incorrectly can produce invalid impedance or S-parameter results. Confirm the port orientation and the reference plane before trusting the result.

For an alternative setup, CST may support a discrete port. Use it only when the excitation and reference impedance are defined correctly for the chosen model.

19. Mesh settings

Step 14 — Set the mesh

The mesh determines how the electromagnetic fields are discretized.

3dswym.3dexperience.3ds.com

Why mesh matters

Your design contains:

  • Thin copper layers

  • A 1.6 mm substrate

  • Narrow slots

  • Feed line

  • Radiation boundaries

If the mesh is too coarse, the slot and feed geometry may not be represented accurately.

Recommended workflow

  1. Use automatic mesh settings initially.

  2. Check the mesh around the slot, feed, and substrate.

  3. Refine the mesh where necessary.

  4. Run a convergence check.

Do not choose a fixed mesh cell size blindly. CST's adaptive mesh features and solver-specific mesh controls should be used to ensure that the result is stable.

Rule: A result that changes significantly when the mesh is refined is not ready to be treated as a final result.

Step 15 — Start the simulation

Before running:

Simulation checklist

Run

  1. Save the project.

  2. Start the solver.

  3. Wait until the simulation finishes.

  4. Open the S-parameter results.

Do not assume the simulation is successful merely because it finishes without an error. Inspect the results for physical plausibility and setup errors.

21. Analyze S11 (return loss)

Step 16 — Open the S11 result

S11 describes the reflection at port 1.

The return loss in dB is commonly plotted as:

20log⁡10∣S11∣20\log_{10}|S_{11}|20log10​∣S11​∣

A more negative value indicates less reflected power.

electronics.stackexchange.com

What to check

Your graph should be inspected for resonant dips near:

  • 2.4 GHz

  • 5.0 GHz

A commonly used impedance-matching criterion is:

S11≤−10 dBS_{11}\leq-10\text{ dB}S11​≤−10 dB

This corresponds to a reflection coefficient magnitude of 0.316 or less.

Do not claim that both bands meet −10 dB until your actual CST results confirm it.

Step 17 — VSWR result

Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) indicates impedance matching.

For a reflection coefficient magnitude ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣:

VSWR≤2VSWR\leq2VSWR≤2

25. Optimize the antenna

Step 20 — Dual-band optimization

This is the most important part of the project.

Your initial design is unlikely to have both exact target resonances and good impedance matching immediately. Optimization is normal in antenna design.

Parameters to tune

1. Patch length

Changes the primary resonant frequency. Adjust the patch length to shift the lower resonance.

2. Slot length

Changes the slot-related current path and affects the higher resonance.

3. Feed position

Changes the input impedance and impedance matching.

4. Slot width and separation

Affects coupling, bandwidth, and the resonant behavior of the slot structure.

Tuning rules

Observation

First parameter to investigate

Lower resonance too low

Reduce patch length

Lower resonance too high

Increase patch length

Upper resonance too low

Adjust slot geometry

Upper resonance too high

Adjust slot geometry

Resonance exists but matching is poor

Feed position or matching structure

Resonances interact strongly

Slot dimensions and feed coupling

These are starting tuning directions. The exact response depends on the geometry and mode behavior.

CST optimization workflow

  1. Define the geometry parameters.

  2. Create parameter sweeps for patch length and slot length.

  3. Run the simulation across the selected values.

  4. Inspect S11.

  5. Select promising geometry values.

  6. Refine the parameter range.

  7. Run a final mesh-converged simulation.

You can use CST's built-in optimizer if your license supports it. Set goals such as:

  • Low S11 near 2.4 GHz.

  • Low S11 near 5.0 GHz.

  • Acceptable gain and efficiency.

  • Practical fabrication dimensions.

Do not optimize only S11. A design with a deep S11 notch but poor efficiency or an unwanted radiation mode may not be useful for your application.

26. Fabrication of the antenna

After the simulated antenna meets your design requirements, prepare the PCB layout.

Step 21 — Export the layout

Possible workflow:

  1. Finalize the patch and slot dimensions in CST.

  2. Check the top copper pattern and ground dimensions.

  3. Export or recreate the geometry in a PCB design tool.

  4. Verify the dimensions in millimeters.

  5. Prepare the manufacturing file, such as Gerber, if your fabrication service requires it.

Do not fabricate the initial unoptimized geometry. First confirm the simulated dual-band behavior and check the feed and connector design.

27. SMA connector installation

Step 24 — Attach the SMA connector

etsy.com

A suitable SMA edge connector or PCB RF connector should be selected according to the board edge, thickness, and feed geometry.

Procedure

  1. Verify the connector is rated for the operating frequencies.

  2. Position the connector on the PCB edge.

  3. Align the center pin with the microstrip feed.

  4. Ensure the connector ground contacts connect correctly to the ground plane.

  5. Solder carefully.

  6. Inspect the joint for shorts and poor solder connections.

The connector geometry can significantly affect the measurement. A poor connection can produce a misleading S11 result.

28. Measurement using a VNA

Step 25 — Calibrate the Vector Network Analyzer

hamradiobase.com

A VNA measures reflection and transmission characteristics.

For a one-port antenna measurement, S11 is the primary measurement.

Procedure

  1. Switch on the VNA.

  2. Set the frequency range to cover the target bands, for example 1.8–6.0 GHz if supported.

  3. Select the appropriate one-port calibration.

  4. Perform calibration using the correct standards:

    • Open

    • Short

    • Load

  5. Connect the antenna using a suitable cable or connector.

  6. Measure S11.

Use the calibration method recommended by your VNA manufacturer. Calibration plane and connector repeatability matter.

End-to-end

  1. Literature review

    Study dual-band microstrip patch antenna designs.

  2. Design calculations

    Calculate the initial patch dimensions for 2.4 GHz.

  3. CST geometry

    Create substrate, ground, patch, feed, and slot.

  4. Simulation

    Configure ports, boundaries, mesh, and solver.

  5. Optimization

    Tune the patch and slot for both frequency bands.

  6. Final design

    Verify S11, VSWR, gain, and radiation patterns.

  7. Fabrication

    Manufacture the PCB and install the SMA connector.

  8. Measurement

    Calibrate the VNA and measure the antenna.

  9. Comparison and report

    Compare simulated and measured performance.

31. Project report structure

You can use the following chapters for your mini-project report.

01

Introduction

Overview of microstrip patch antennas, dual-band operation, and applications.

02

Literature Review

Review previous dual-band antenna designs and their methods.

03

Design Methodology

Explain the substrate, patch calculations, slot geometry, and feed design.

04

CST Simulation

Explain the geometry, boundary conditions, mesh, port, and solver.

05

Results and Discussion

Show S11, VSWR, gain, efficiency, and radiation patterns.

06

Fabrication and Measurement

Describe PCB manufacturing, connector attachment, VNA calibration, and measurements.

07

Conclusion and Future Scope

Summarize actual findings and possible improvements.

32. Common CST errors and solutions

Problem

Possible cause

What to check

No resonance near 2.4 GHz

Patch dimensions or material mismatch

Patch length, substrate permittivity

No resonance near 5 GHz

Slot geometry not supporting a suitable mode

Slot dimensions, current distribution, coupling

Very high S11

Poor feed matching

Feed position, port setup, impedance

Simulation error

Invalid geometry or solver setup

Overlapping objects, mesh, boundaries

Strange radiation pattern

Incorrect far-field setup or geometry

Monitor frequency, orientation, boundaries

Measured and simulated results differ

Fabrication or connector effects

Substrate, SMA connection, calibration

Truth: Getting a dual-band antenna to work is not just drawing two slots and running the solver. The design needs iterative electromagnetic analysis. If your first design does not show 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz resonances, that is a normal engineering problem to solve—not a reason to fabricate it immediately.

  • RF Toolbox — useful for RF/S-parameter analysis.

  • MATLAB — calculations, scripts, plots, data processing.

The important point

If your project title is:

Design and Fabrication of a Dual-Band Microstrip Patch Antenna for 2.4/5 GHz

I recommend:

CST = primary antenna design and electromagnetic simulation

MATLAB = mathematical analysis + optimization + result visualization

Don't make the mistake of designing the whole antenna only in MATLAB and claiming CST-level electromagnetic simulation. MATLAB can model antennas with Antenna Toolbox, but CST gives you a different full-wave 3D simulation environment.

STEP 1 — Set up MATLAB for the Dual-Band Antenna Project

Project

Design and Fabrication of a Dual-Band Microstrip Patch Antenna for 2.4/5 GHz

In MATLAB, our first job is to verify that the required antenna tools are installed and then create a clean project workspace.

1.1 Open MATLAB

Open MATLAB.

You should see something similar to:

  • Current Folder
  • Command Window
  • Workspace
  • Editor

1.2 Check your MATLAB version

In the Command Window, type:

matlab
version

Press Enter.

You should get something similar to:

Plain text
MATLAB Version: 25.2.0...

Your exact version may be different.

Also run:

matlab
ver

This displays the installed products/toolboxes.

1.3 Check Antenna Toolbox

This project will use Antenna Toolbox.

In the Command Window, enter:

matlab
ver Antenna_Toolbox

If installed

You should see something similar to:

Plain text
Antenna Toolbox Version ...

Good. Continue.

If MATLAB says something like:

Plain text
'ver' cannot find the product ...

or Antenna Toolbox is not listed, stop here.

You need to install/activate Antenna Toolbox before proceeding with the antenna-design portion.

Run:

matlab

Plain text

1.5 Check Optimization Toolbox

Now run this:

matlab

Plain text

Plain text

Very important

The patchMicrostrip object we created here is only a test.

We have not designed the actual 2.4/5 GHz dual-band antenna yet.

The next step will be Step 2 — Mathematical design calculations in MATLAB, where we calculate:

  • WWW — patch width
  • LLL — patch length
  • ϵeff\epsilon_{eff}ϵeff​ — effective dielectric constant
  • ΔL\Delta LΔL — fringing-field extension
  • LeffL_{eff}Leff​ — effective length
  • substrate dimensions
  • approximate feed dimensions

Then we'll use those calculated values to create the actual antenna model, rather than guessing dimensions.
